Fourteen studies were included, most of them uncontrolled before-after evaluations of local schemes. Eleven reported improved wellbeing scores after referral, but only two had a comparison group and neither found a clear difference. Attrition between referral and follow-up exceeded 40 percent in half the studies. We judged the evidence insufficient to show that link worker social prescribing improves wellbeing, and we call for controlled evaluations with complete follow-up."},{"title":"Link worker social prescribing and primary care consultation rates: a systematic review and meta-analysis","authors":"Achterberg-Nkemelu J, Sorensen-Pike A, Dasgupta-Rowe M","year":2021,"venue":"Primary Care Services Research","doi":"10.5555/pcsr.2021.0240","providerType":"review","abstract":"We included nine controlled studies of link worker social prescribing that reported primary care consultations. Pooled across seven studies, consultation rates at 12 months were 15 percent lower after referral than in comparison groups (rate ratio 0.85, 95 percent CI 0.74 to 0.98), with substantial heterogeneity. Comparison groups were usually patients who were not referred, and only one study was randomised. Effects were larger in studies of frequent attenders, where regression to the mean is likely. We rate the certainty of evidence as low."},{"title":"Effects of social prescribing on loneliness: a systematic review of controlled studies","authors":"Kowalski-Asante B, Lindgren-Oyelaran P, Moreau-Tanaka E","year":2022,"venue":"Journal of Loneliness and Social Health","doi":"10.5555/jlsh.2022.0077","providerType":"review","abstract":"We identified seven controlled studies of social prescribing that measured loneliness, including two randomised trials. The pooled effect on loneliness was small and uncertain (standardised mean difference -0.08, 95 percent CI -0.21 to 0.05). Participants valued the relationship with the link worker, but the activities they were referred to were often unavailable or too far away. Studies rarely reported how many referrals led to sustained participation in community activities. Certainty was low because of imprecision and risk of bias, and follow-up rarely extended beyond six months."},{"title":"Economic evaluations of social prescribing: a systematic review","authors":"Pellegrino-Adjei S, Hartley-Nakashima K","year":2020,"venue":"Health Economics and Community Care","providerType":"review","abstract":"We reviewed six economic evaluations of social prescribing schemes. Four reported savings from fewer GP and emergency department attendances, but all used before-after comparisons without a control group, and savings disappeared in the one analysis that adjusted for regression to the mean. Costs of the voluntary sector activities that patients were referred to were rarely counted. We conclude that claims of net savings are not supported by robust evidence and that future evaluations should include community sector costs and a comparison group."},{"title":"Who is referred to social prescribing and who benefits? A realist review","authors":"Oduya-Fairweather C, Brandt-Solis M","year":2023,"venue":"Community Health and Wellbeing Reviews","doi":"10.5555/chwr.2023.0305","providerType":"review","abstract":"Drawing on 48 documents, we developed programme theories for how link worker social prescribing works. Benefits depended on link workers having enough time to build trust, on available and affordable community activities, and on the person's readiness to engage. People with complex needs, such as debt, insecure housing and severe mental illness, often needed many more contacts and were more likely to disengage when referred onward too quickly. The review cannot estimate effect sizes but explains why averages may hide very different outcomes for different groups."},{"title":"Overlap of primary studies across systematic reviews of social prescribing: a citation matrix analysis","authors":"Varga-Lindqvist T, Ebuka-Harrington S","year":2024,"venue":"Research Synthesis Methods Notes","doi":"10.5555/rsmn.2024.0019","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We built a citation matrix of the primary studies included in 11 systematic reviews of social prescribing published between 2017 and 2023. The reviews included 97 unique primary studies, and the corrected covered area was 18 percent, indicating very high overlap. Six small uncontrolled evaluations were included in eight or more reviews. Reviews reaching positive conclusions leaned more heavily on these evaluations than reviews reaching uncertain conclusions. We recommend that overviews count each primary study once and report conclusions against a citation matrix."},{"title":"Social prescribing: an overview of systematic reviews","authors":"Nakamura-Blackwood R, Adebayo-Strand J","year":2018,"venue":"Primary Care Evidence Summaries","doi":"10.5555/pces.2018.0044","providerType":"review","abstract":"We searched for systematic reviews of social prescribing to March 2017 and found five, all of low or critically low quality. The reviews agreed that participants reported feeling better but disagreed on effects on service use. None of the reviews assessed overlap between their included studies, and none separated link worker models from direct referral by clinicians. We conclude that the evidence was insufficient to support or reject investment and recommend an updated overview once controlled studies are published, with an assessment of overlap."}]}
